claims.text: The as-cast eutectic HEA contains multiple chemically distinct phases.
The phases form an interpenetrating microstructure.
Protective oxide layers are pre-formed specifically at the phase boundaries of the as-cast alloy.
Oxide layers can protect an HEA against elevated-temperature wear.
Mechanical wear preferentially removes or disrupts protective oxide films at phase boundaries.
Wear-induced oxide removal exposes chemically active underlying phases.
Micro-galvanic coupling between phases accelerates selective localized corrosion in a eutectic HEA.
The body-centered-cubic phase can undergo selective dissolution in molten salt because of interphase micro-galvanic coupling.
Raising temperature increases chemical degradation of the eutectic HEA.
High temperature destabilizes phase interfaces and exacerbates oxide-scale breakdown.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion produce total degradation greater than the sum of independently measured wear and corrosion.
Interfacial coating or tailored heat treatment will stabilize the boundary oxide layer and reduce galvanic potential differences.
The untreated baseline will exhibit greater total degradation and greater local corrosion and wear losses than the reinforced material.
Reinforcing phase boundaries will reduce both wear damage and corrosion rate.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate at approximately 800–900 °C under simultaneous mechanical loading and corrosive exposure.
A controlled comparison uses untreated as-cast and boundary-reinforced samples under identical temperature, load, and corrosive-environment conditions.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome wording says 'compared to a standard as-cast sample, the baseline alloy' will show accelerated degradation, but the baseline is itself defined as the untreated standard as-cast alloy. The intended comparison appears to be untreated versus reinforced samples.
